To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the degradation of toluene, m-xylene, and benzaldehyde in an aquifer column was coupled with the reductive transformation of nitrate to nitrogen and that benzoate was identified as a metabolite of toluene.
toluene and other alkylated benzens can be mineralized in a denitrifying aquifer column.
toluene and xylene were mineralized in an anoxic aquifer column, that nitrate was the terminal electron acceptor, and that nitrous oxide was also a suitable electron acceptor for toluene degradation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the degradation of aromatic hydrocarbons in the absence of oxygen and with the elucidation of the microbial mechanisms involved.
the development of new biotechnological methods for the in situ bioremediation of contaminated aquifers.
the biodegradation of organic pollutants in aquifers and the role of nitrate and other electron acceptors in the degradation of hydrocarbon contaminants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anaerobic degradation of toluene is a two-step process.
the mineralization of toluene, xylene, and other alkylbenzenes is possible under anaerobic conditions, provided that nitrate or nitrous oxide is available as electron acceptor.
the degradation of toluene in a denitrifying laboratory-scale aquifer column can be described by the following equation: C7H8 + 2.5 NO3- + 2 H+ = 2 CO2 + 1.5 N2 + 4 H2O + 2.25 NO2-.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nitrate reduction is a suitable alternative for the in situ remediation of groundwater polluted by aromatic compounds.
the degradation of toluene, m-xylene, benzaldehyde and benzoate in denitrifying aquifer columns was coupled with the dissimilatory reduction of nitrate and nitrous oxide.
anaerobic degradation of hydrocarbons in the subsurface is a complex process involving a variety of different microorganisms, and the degradation potential of an aquifer is highly site specific.
The main takeaway from our work is that
nitrous oxide is an attractive electron acceptor for in situ bioremediation of aromatic pollutants.
the use of nitrous oxide as a surrogate electron acceptor may offer attractive options to remediate contaminated groundwater aquifers.
nitrate and nitrous oxide can serve as terminal electron acceptors for anaerobic degradation of toluene, m-xylene, and benzoate.
